papers.title: On Modelling the Scattering of Highly Nonlinear Transient Water Waves Due to Surface-Piercing Cylinder. Part I: Formulations and Verifications
papers.abstract: The presence of extreme ocean waves poses substantial threats to the safety of marine engineering applications and navigational activities. Accurate prediction of the nonlinear wave loads on offshore structures in large-diameter cylindrical configuration, such as monopile wind turbines and platform columns, requires a robust solution to the high-order wave diffraction problem. This paper introduces a novel, highly nonlinear time-domain numerical pseudo-spectrum model based on potential flow theory. By leveraging the Fredholm integral equation of the second kind and Legendre polynomials, a distinct efficient solver for computing the velocity potential on the cylinder surface and vertical velocity at free surface is developed. The present method is verified by comparing with a direct approach based on Fourier transform and established theoretical models for simulating the scattering of small steepness uniform waves. The convergence and computational efficiency of the present method is also demonstrated. The validation of the new model for simulating highly nonlinear transient water waves will be reported in Part II. The proposed model provides a powerful and efficient new framework for analyzing high-order nonlinear wave diffraction and hydrodynamic loads, with significant implications for both scientific research and the engineering design of coastal and offshore structures.

papers.title: Generation of extreme waves with flexible features in fully nonlinear wave models
papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. We consider the generation of extreme waves of flexible features in deep-water surface gravity waves, in the context of the fully nonlinear wave model, i.e. Euler equations of the free surface. This is achieved through a recently developed GenWave approach, coupled with the high-order spectral method to solve the Euler equations. Through an iterative refinement procedure, GenWave progressively refines the initial phases associated with a given wave spectrum, which leads to extreme-wave generation at specified design time and location, with their probability of exceedance quantified. In this study, we consider two types of extreme waves, enabled by the flexibility of GenWave. The first type is a spatially and temporally localised rogue wave, and second is a spatially localised extreme-wave group propagating at a constant speed. The two generated extreme-wave profiles are compared with their prototypes – the Peregrine soliton and regular soliton (or bright soliton) in the context of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS), with reasonable agreement. For the persistent group, comparison with linear evolution and the NLS identifies nonlinear persistence, faster propagation and bound-wave content beyond the leading-order NLS description.

papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. We investigate the evolution of Peregrine breather (PB) rogue waves in narrow-banded random background wave fields using a fully nonlinear wave model. The influence of the peak wavenumber, the significant wave height, and the spectral width of the background field on the maximum crest height, the timing of rogue wave occurrence, and the spatiotemporal distribution of rogue waves is analysed. The results show that when the background peak wavenumber matches that of the PB carrier, nonlinear focusing is enhanced and the phase distribution is modified. The maximum crest height increases by 4.4 % on average, the mean time of first occurrence decreases by 15.9 %, and rogue wave activity extends over a larger spatiotemporal domain. These effects weaken as the wavenumber detuning increases. Increasing the significant wave height of the background field enhances nonlinear interactions and leads to more pronounced changes in the relative phases among wave components, resulting in broader distributions of rogue waves. Over the range considered, the ensemble-averaged maximum crest height increases by up to 5.4 %, while the mean time of first occurrence decreases by up to 40.4 %. papers.title: Stochastic interpretation of the Water Waves equations
papers.abstract: The aim of this article is to derive a stochastic interpretation of the Water Waves equations, based on the location uncertainty principle (LU). Next, these equations are used to infer simpler models from scaling limits, such as the Saint-Venant, Boussinesq and Serre-Green-Naghdi ones. Once adapted to the stochastic setting, these models have been successfully implemented numerically, and we show several experiments to assess their properties -- for example the breaking of the wave symmetry, and the influence of time correlated noises.

papers.title: Directional and geometric characteristics of breaking-wave whitecaps in a laboratory wave basin
papers.abstract: The directional characteristics of wave breaking are essential for understanding surface wave dynamics. However, the directional representation of breaking in spectral wave models remains poorly constrained by experimental observations. This study analyzes breaking waves using image processing of whitecaps to extract crest-normal directions and geometric properties. The lower boundary of each active whitecap was used as a proxy for the local breaking-wave crest, with the associated direction defined as normal to the estimated crest. Whitecaps were identified and tracked across multiple cases, and the distribution of their crest-normal directions was compared with the directional spectrum of the wave field. The results indicate that narrower spectral distributions are associated with more focused distributions of crest-normal directions, demonstrating a correspondence between wave directional spreading and the directional organization of breaking crests. Geometric analysis further indicates a power-law relationship between whitecap area and crest length, which warrants further investigation across a broader range of conditions. These findings provide insight into the relationship between breaking-crest geometry and the directional properties of the wave spectrum.

papers.title: Modeling wave attenuation by depth-induced breaking in a pseudo-spectral model
papers.abstract: Climate change and the increasing frequency of extreme weather events pose significant threats to coastal infrastructure, necessitating accurate numerical tools for simulating coastal wave dynamics. Pseudo-spectral models based on the fully nonlinear potential flow theory offer high physical fidelity and computational efficiency for this purpose. The model is extensively validated against benchmark laboratory experiments involving regular and irregular waves over various two-dimensional and three-dimensional topographies, including steep slopes, submerged bars, and underwater lenses. papers.title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation
papers.abstract: The state space of a dynamical system can, under suitable conditions, be reconstructed from a single observational time-series through delay-coordinate embedding. However, reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse measurements remains a considerable challenge. Here, by combining deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity properties of unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation, we show that the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field can be reconstructed from observations collected at a {\it single} measurement location. We subsequently use these reconstructions to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics from point observations obtained in controlled water wave tank experiments, demonstrating excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field. Our results show that extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations and provide a framework that may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.

papers.abstract: We investigate fully nonlinear water waves and fluid-particle dynamics generated by the horizontal motion of a seabed obstacle with prescribed time-dependent velocity. papers.title: Simulation of Breaking Waves in OpenFOAM: Numerical Assessment Using Stokes Wave Initial Conditions
papers.abstract: Understanding the characteristics of breaking waves in deep and intermediate water is essential for both air–sea interaction and wave-structure interaction. This paper explores optimal numerical methods for modelling breaking events within the OpenFOAM framework, using a 2D numerical wave tank. The present work discusses the implementation of initial wave conditions in the OpenFOAM framework and the optimal combination of numerical techniques used for modelling breaking events. Stokes wave theory is used to prescribe the initial wave field, which is first assessed against the corresponding analytical solution before the subsequent nonlinear evolution and breaking processes are investigated. Three orders of Stokes wave theory are used to investigate their capability in simulating wave propagation and modeling a single breaking wave event. Various numerical schemes implemented in OpenFOAM are tested to determine the optimal combination for achieving accurate results. The findings demonstrate that fifth-order Stokes wave theory is the most suitable for capturing the highly nonlinear evolution of waves leading up to breaking.

papers.title: A quantitative measure of predictability for surface gravity waves
papers.abstract: We introduce a Bayesian inference framework to characterize the predictability of a one dimensional ocean surface wave field given surface elevation measurements from a sensor. Unlike the classical theories that only sketch the boundary of a predictable zone based on group velocity, we use the Bayesian posterior uncertainty of surface elevation to quantify the local predictability at every spatiotemporal location. Our approach first constructs a prior distribution to encode existing knowledge of the wave field such as the spectrum and propagation direction. By conditioning on the (possibly noisy) measurement data, we infer the posterior distribution of the wave field, from which a spatiotemporal uncertainty map is extracted. This map agrees well with the group-velocity-based classical predictable zone theory when the frequency spectrum has bounded support. Meanwhile, it also demonstrates predictability even for a spectrum with unbounded frequency support where the classical predictable zone degenerates. A refined analysis of posterior uncertainty using observability Gramian matrix reveals a `data-informed'part and an `un-informed'part of the wave field, with the latter being fundamentally un-predictable. papers.title: Free-surface breaking dynamics and morphology of waves generated by the semi-submerged wedge-shaped body
papers.abstract: The breaking waves at the bow and stern represent a fundamental free-surface phenomenon involving violent interface deformation, air entrainment, and strong two-phase coupling. The temporal evolution and spatial distribution of wave breaking are fundamental to understanding water-air mixing flows around ships. The present study adopts the square stern of high-speed ships as a reference and selects a wedge model as the research object in order to investigate the characteristics of interface breaking and the flow morphology. The free-surface waves around the wedge model were measured using a binocular vision system. A systematic analysis was conducted to investigate the impact of various parameters on the flow patterns in the bow and stern regions. The parameters investigated included draft depth (D), stern width (B), attack angle (α), and draft Froude number FrD=U/gD. The results show that the wave profiles have strong similarity when FrD is chosen as the dominant parameter. The associated parameters of FrD and geometric parameters are found to have a significant influence on the morphological characteristics of the waves.

papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. What do the ocean surface and a swaying flag have in common? Both are deformable surfaces exhibiting chaotic motion when exposed to turbulent flows. Whether such motion is primarily driven by flow turbulence or by nonlinear dynamics intrinsic to the surface remains debated. papers.title: Extended nonlinear theory for water wave modulations under strong winds
papers.abstract: The fourth-order weakly nonlinear theory for modulated wind waves has been derived for a nonlinear-generalized Miles' surface pressure term. The situation of unidirectional waves and a strong wind is considered. The focus is made on the conditions of great and intermediate water depths. Dynamic effects associated with the nonlinear character of the wind–wave interaction have been identified, such as the saturation or intensification of the wind–wave energy exchange, the alteration of the wave and wavegroup shapes including modification of the nonlinear induced flow when the depth is finite, and the complicated picture of the modulational instability. We suggest that a sudden change in wind intensity or direction may contribute to the occurrence of rogue waves due to the wind-dependent bound waves.

papers.abstract: The Arabian Sea Great Whirl (GW) is a large, quasi‐stationary anticyclonic eddy that develops under the southwest monsoon, combining strong surface‐current shear with an energetic and seasonally organized wavefield. This setting provides a distinctive natural laboratory for examining wave–current interactions beyond the transient mid‐latitude regimes emphasized in previous work. Here we ask whether the GW produces a coherent and observable significant‐wave‐height (SWH) footprint, how the relative orientation of waves and currents controls its asymmetry, and how monsoon wind forcing regulates the relative importance of wind‐driven wave growth and current‐induced modulation. We combine multi‐satellite observations with SWAN (Simulating Waves Nearshore) numerical simulations to address these questions. The GW exhibits an asymmetric SWH pattern, with lower SWH where waves and currents align and higher SWH where they oppose, consistent with current‐induced refraction and wave‐energy redistribution. Wave–current modulation strengthens when eddy‐current gradients dominate the background wavefield, while stronger wind‐wave growth diminishes the current signature. papers.abstract: The interaction between internal solitary waves (ISWs) and ice cover is an important process governing wave deformation, energy dissipation, and mixing in polar oceans. In this study, laboratory experiments were conducted in a strongly stratified silicone oil–water two-layer system using a rigid, nondeformable ice-cover model to examine the combined effects of ice-cover position and incident-wave amplitude on ISW evolution. Five dimensionless ice-cover positions and four incident-wave amplitudes were considered. Image-based interface extraction, particle image velocimetry, and wavelet analysis were used to quantify waveform evolution, spatial amplitude attenuation, spectral redistribution, and flow-field responses. The results show that the vertical position of the ice cover strongly regulates the transition of ISWs from stable propagation to instability-dominated evolution. Four representative regimes were identified: wave flattening, wave reflection, interfacial instability, and wave breaking. papers.title: New third-order probability density function for the surface elevation in irregular seas
papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. We develop saddle-point approximations of the probability density function (PDF) for the surface elevation in nonlinear, irregular seas, without any assumptions regarding uni-directionality of the wave field or narrow-bandedness of the spectrum. A new, closed-form approximation of the PDF at third order is derived, accounting for both skewness and kurtosis. The approximate PDF matches known asymptotics of the third-order positive tail exactly and is free of unphysical oscillations in the negative tail, which widely plague existing PDFs describing nonlinear seas. A normalisation procedure is introduced to enforce unit integral, zero mean and unit variance. We further show that the input cumulants can be adjusted to likewise yield prescribed skewness and kurtosis. Comparison of the new third-order PDF against challenging datasets stemming from irregular wave theory, a fully nonlinear wave model as well as laboratory experiments establishes accuracy. In the Appendix we additionally develop a novel perturbation method, which is used to derive the full form of the asymptotic positive and negative tails at fourth and fifth order, including (previously unknown) prefactors. Collectively, it is shown that even-order solutions inevitably involve oscillatory negative tails, whereas odd orders admit non-oscillatory negative-tail solutions.

papers.title: Lagrangian transport resulting from superposition of surface gravity waves and an internal solitary wave
papers.abstract: Particle transport at the ocean surface is governed by oceanic flows of different scales. In this study, we numerically investigate the collective impact of surface gravity waves (SGWs) and an internal solitary wave (ISW) on free-surface particle transport. By carrying out wave-phase-resolved simulations, we show that adding SGW-induced Stokes drift to the ISW-induced particle displacement acting in isolation does not accurately estimate the displacement resulting from the combined effect of SGWs and the ISW. The ISW-only prediction underestimates the actual ISW-associated displacement by 30–46% in co-propagating configurations and overestimates its magnitude by 200–350% in counter-propagating configurations. The contact time, i.e., the duration for which the particle transport is affected by the ISW-induced current, is found to be longer when SGWs and the ISW co-propagate and shorter for counter-propagation cases with the same ISW magnitude. This asymmetry reveals two distinct mechanisms: the Lagrangian velocities are not additive, and the ISW-modulated SGW orbital velocities and resulting Stokes drift alter the effective drift along the particle trajectories.

papers.title: Modulational stability of finite-depth Stokes waves with constant vorticity
papers.abstract: We investigate the effect of constant vorticity on the modulational spectral stability of small-amplitude periodic gravity waves for the two-dimensional finite-depth water-wave system. We derive an explicit stability criterion that agrees with the prediction obtained by Thomas, Kharif and Manna [43] through a nonlinear Schr\"odinger approximation. For waves propagating to the right, we identify a sharp range of dimensionless positive (counterclockwise) vorticity, for which modulational instability is suppressed at every depth, while at any fixed depth sufficiently strong negative (clockwise) vorticity also restores modulational stability. We give a complete description of the spectrum near the origin and identify a figure-eight spectral curve in the unstable regime. A key distinction from the irrotational case is that the usual Hamiltonian factorization of the linearized operator fails at zero Floquet exponent on the full periodic Sobolev space. We therefore carry out a spectral reduction based on reversibility, without relying on Hamiltonian factorization.

papers.title: On the spectra of strong turbulence on water surfaces
papers.abstract: Here, I give a brief history of the theory, with twists and turns, and list possible predictions for the spectra of the direct cascade of gravity waves on the water. The description of long waves is straightforward within the weak-turbulence theory developed by Zakharov and his school. As the energy cascade proceeds to shorter scales, the mean surface steepness grows, and wave-breaking events appear with increasing frequency. Considering surface cusps, Phillips suggested a wavenumber spectrum (with a wrong magnitude, as I argue here) and a frequency spectrum whose whole form is incorrect. The right form for the frequency spectral slope due to breaking waves was suggested by Kuznetsov. Here we estimate the magnitude and argue that the frequency spectrum is expected to continue unchanged through the whole cascade. The transition from weak to strong turbulence in the wavenumber and spatio-temporal spectra is due to spectrally nonlocal interactions and happens earlier (at larger scales) than the dimensional estimate suggests. As a result, the magnitude of the strong-turbulence spectrum is not universal but depends on the pumping for a sufficiently long weak-turbulence cascade. The reason for nonlocality is likely that breaking of shorter waves is determined by the magnitude of the longest wave on whose crest they are running.

papers.abstract: Wave breaking plays a central role in ocean dynamics, dissipating wave energy and shaping the evolution of the sea surface. Yet, breaking remains difficult to model: envelope‐based models efficiently capture nonlinear wave evolution and are interpretable but exclude breaking, while high‐fidelity direct numerical simulations resolve breaking dynamics but are too computationally demanding for large domains and long timescales. This is enabled by training on high‐resolution Reynolds‐averaged Navier‐Stokes simulations. papers.venue: Proceedings of the European Wave and Tidal Energy Conference
papers.abstract: Extreme load analysis is an essential step in the design of structural and mooring systems for wave energy converters (WEC). The current study aims to evaluate the structural loads on the MARMOK Oscillating Water Column (OWC) WEC under both regular and irregular wave conditions, as well as to evaluate the effectiveness of its station keeping (mooring) systems. The project employs the open source computational fluid dynamics simulation software OpenFOAM to model the fully moored floating system. The WEC device hydrodynamics are validated against laboratory data for free decay in heave and pitch motions. In addition, the station keeping model is validated against mooring tension static offset tests and benchmarked against experimental data in irregular waves. An elegant method of numerically recreating irregular wave inflow conditions from empirical measurements is shown which allows for consistent comparison between the model and experimental results. The calibrated numerical model is then employed to study the full-scale system’s responses. Preliminary results of structural loadings on the fixed and floating spar buoy (with one mooring configuration as sample) are presented in the paper.

papers.abstract: Landslide-generated impulse waves are a typical secondary hydrodynamic hazard in mountainous river-type reservoirs and exhibit pronounced nonlinear characteristics. However, the mechanisms by which mainstream–tributary confluence flows modulate wave dynamics in the generation region remain insufficiently understood. To elucidate the wave-response characteristics of granular landslide-generated impulse waves under confluence conditions, three-dimensional physical model tests were conducted. Time–frequency analysis, empirical correlations, and free-surface waveform modeling were then combined to investigate wave types, spatial responses, and free-surface evolution in the wave-generation region. The impulse waves were dominated by nonlinear oscillatory and nonlinear transitional waves, with dominant frequencies concentrated at 1–2 Hz. Increasing landslide velocity, relative landslide thickness, and entry angle promoted the transition toward nonlinear transitional waves. The free-surface response exhibited pronounced directionality, with the largest amplitude occurring directly in front of the landslide, followed by the upstream region, and the smallest occurring downstream. papers.title: Scale effects on wave forces and flow structures around a perforated semicircular submerged breakwater
papers.abstract: Perforated semicircular submerged breakwaters can attenuate incident waves while allowing water exchange, making them suitable for coastal protection and marine infrastructure. Their hydraulic performance is often assessed using physical models based on Froude similarity, for which Reynolds similarity cannot be preserved. Extrapolating wave loads from reduced models to prototype conditions may therefore introduce bias. To quantify this effect, a validated numerical wave flume was used to examine six geometric scale ratios ( λ L = 1, 5, 10, 15, 25, and 35), four perforation rates ( ϵ = 0–15%), and five wave conditions. Validation used measurements from physical model experiments and field pressures obtained at prototype scale. Comparisons considered horizontal force coefficients, free surface elevations, velocity fields, and vorticity fields. Smaller models increasingly overestimated the shoreward peak force. At λ L = 35 and ϵ = 10%, the mean model to prototype ratio of the shoreward peak force coefficient reached 1.23. The differences between model and prototype responses were mainly associated with changes in wave transmission, reverse flow, and vortical motion over and behind the structure as scale decreased. These findings improve the interpretation of reduced model results and support more reliable prototype extrapolation of wave loads on perforated submerged structures.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical simulations of near resonant 2D soliton interaction in shallow water
papers.abstract: Experiments were carried out in {a} large wave basin ($27\times 30$\,m$^2$) to study the interactions of non-linear waves in shallow water (0.35\,m deep). A stereoscopic technique was used to measure the waves accurately over a vast area ($180$\,m$^2$). The numerical code {Tolosa-lct}, designed for simulating wave propagation in shallow water, reproduces the observations and extends the analysis for larger domains. The diffraction of oblique solitons is discussed. Mach interaction of two solitons occurs for some given incidence and amplitudes, producing a third soliton. A focus is made on the near resonant interaction of a soliton with a vertical wall. An example of a regular Mach interaction is shown, where a steady solution is achieved experimentally, with a maximum amplitude amplification of 3.2 at the wall.

papers.venue: Uchenye Zapiski Kazanskogo Universiteta. Seriya Fiziko-Matematicheskie Nauki
papers.abstract: This article examines the applicability of the mesh-free Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) method for numerical simulation of surfable solitary waves propagating over an artificial seabed in a wave pool. The simulations were performed using DualSPHysics, with particular attention given to the accurate reproduction of the free-surface profile. The wave crest overturning, which is highly sensitive to the accuracy of the numerical method, was considered separately. A series of computations was carried out for different bottom geometries and a range of Froude numbers to assess the influence of depth and kinematic parameters on the process of wave formation. The reliability of the SPH approach was verified through additional simulations in OpenFOAM using the finite-volume framework (VOF + RANS). The obtained numerical results were consistent with published experimental data, indicating that SPH simulation can be used for analyzing and optimizing bottom geometry in surf-pool design.

papers.abstract: In this paper, the nonlinear wave dynamics of the (3+1)-dimensional P-type model are investigated using a symbolic neural-network-based hybrid technique. The model is considered in the context of nonlinear wave propagation, which is of practical importance in different areas. This approach combines the modified generalized Riccati equation mapping method with a neural network structure, where each neuron in the first hidden layer represents a Riccati-based activation function, which allows the construction of new physics-based trial solutions. This approach allows the systematic generation of exact traveling wave solutions in space and time. Solutions including solitary waves, and periodic and localized pulses are obtained, which provide essential insight into the influence of model parameters on wave profiles and evolution in complex media. The dynamics of the waves are illustrated by two-dimensional, three-dimensional, and contour plots, which show the behavior of propagation, localization, and stability. The results demonstrate the method is feasible, efficient, and effective for studying high-dimensional nonlinear systems. This work not only extends the Riccati-based neural network approach to the model but also provides a platform for exploring nonlinear wave behavior in shallow-water flows and other hydraulic engineering problems.

papers.title: Modeling Broad-Frequency-Band Water-Wave Experiments with Generalizations of the Nonlinear Schrodinger Equation
papers.abstract: Waves generated by storms gradually disperse, forming swells that can travel thousands of kilometers across the ocean's surface. The evolution of deep-water swells, which are unaffected by the seafloor, can be modeled by the nonlinear Schrodinger (NLS) equation and its generalizations. These models typically assume that the wave trains are comprised of a narrow band of frequencies. We present measurements from a new series of laboratory experiments in which the broadbandedness is increased and show that generalizations of the NLS equation can accurately model these measurements.

papers.title: Numerical Simulations and Analyses of the Long-Term Characteristics of Ocean Waves in the Bohai Sea Under a Coupling Model
papers.abstract: A coupled WRF–ROMS–SWAN framework is used to investigate the long-term wave characteristics of the Bohai Sea through a 20-year hindcast from 2002 to 2022. The model results are validated against CMEMS current data, field wave measurements, and CCMP wind products, showing good agreement with the reference datasets. Three spatial interpolation methods are compared for reconstructing the wave time series at discrete locations, and distance-squared weighted interpolation (DSWI) provides the best overall performance for the present dataset. The reconstructed records show clear seasonal and interannual variations in the significant wave height, average wavelength, and spectral peak period. Spatially, larger mean and extreme wave parameters occur mainly in the central and eastern offshore areas, while the enclosed inner bays are generally calmer. Weibull, Gumbel, Pearson Type III, and Exponential distributions are further applied to estimate wave conditions for return periods of 1–100 years. The Exponential distribution gives the highest long-period estimates, whereas the Weibull distribution gives the lowest. Wave roses also show clear differences in prevailing wave directions among stations. The results provide long-term wave information for offshore engineering and marine hazard assessment in the Bohai Sea.

papers.title: Ship-as-a-buoy for Phase-resolved Reconstruction of Surface Waves
papers.abstract: We develop a data assimilation framework to address the ``ship-as-a-buoy''problem, i.e., estimation of the wave field from time series of ship motion. Unlike previous algorithms which only provide information of wave spectrum, our approach reconstructs the instantaneous phase-resolved wave field. The full framework includes two steps: the first step to generate an initial (rough) estimation of the wave field using the response-amplitude-operators (RAOs), and the second step to refine the reconstruction using an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) to incorporate the measured motion time series. Together with EnKF in the second step, we model the coupled wave-ship dynamics by a high-order spectral (HOS) method for waves and a Cummins equation for ship motion (although higher-fidelity ship model can be applied). We conduct extensive tests of our method for the case with one ship, and the naturally extended cases with multiple ships or with uncertain parameters in the ship motion model. For all test cases we demonstrate favorable reconstruction of the wave field, which in general further improves with the number of ships available and with uncertain parameters properly estimated. We also provide insights on the successful reconstruction in terms of ensemble correlations between the motion time series and features of the wave field.

papers.title: Nonlinear Release of Subinertial Diurnal Internal Tides Forms Spiral Internal Solitary Waves
papers.abstract: Earth's rotation imposes a dynamical barrier on the free propagation of internal tides at high latitudes, raising questions about the fate of tidal energy poleward of the critical latitude. Satellite observations reveal spiral internal solitary waves (ISWs) along the continental slope of the South Orkney Plateau. Although these waves might be attributed to direct steepening of low‐frequency internal tides, theoretical estimates of their propagation speed are nearly twice those inferred from observations. Using high‐resolution simulations, we resolve this inconsistency by identifying a topographically steered energy cascade: subinertial diurnal internal tides, initially trapped by the slope, undergo nonlinear evolution that generates superinertial harmonics. This frequency upshift allows tidal energy to surpass rotational constraints, radiate offshore, and ultimately evolve into the spiral ISWs. These results identify a distinct energy cascade pathway for internal wave dynamics in polar oceans and demonstrate how tidal energy can be redistributed despite rotational limitations.

papers.title: Shoaling of internal solitary waves over linear slopes with variable topography
papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. This study investigates the influence of variable topography on the kinematics of internal solitary wave shoaling across various breaking regimes under the unifying condition of a slope-intersecting pycnocline. It is demonstrated that bottom corrugations can significantly modify the dynamics: in plunging, collapsing and fission cases, variable topography alters wave shape and induces Kelvin–Helmholtz billows within the pycnocline; in surging scenarios, it impedes upslope propagation and generates a reflected mode-2 wave offshore. Despite these pronounced mechanical effects during the breaking phase, analysis of density and enstrophy fields via a user-defined scatter plot method suggests that potential post-wave mixing distributions remain largely unaffected by changes in the topography parameter, indicating a transient influence confined to the active shoaling region. In the fission case, the length scale of the topography can be much larger than the wavelength. In this case, undulating topography locally modifies layer depths, potentially arresting and restarting the fission process as critical depth ratios are traversed. A comparison between two- and three-dimensional simulations is made in the collapsing case and it is shown that the two-dimensional simulations accurately capture the dynamics of wave breaking at onset.

papers.title: Rogue waves in the dam-break problem for the Kundu--Eckhaus equation
papers.abstract: We study rogue wave formation in the dam-break problem for the Kundu--Eckhaus equation with deterministic and randomly perturbed box initial data. For the unperturbed real box, the gauge transformation and Galilean invariance relate the intensity evolution to that of the focusing nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation. The Kundu--Eckhaus parameter determines the phase, the real shift of the discrete spectrum and the drift velocity. We compare uniform, Gaussian and Laplace perturbations with equal variance and the same correlation scale in the underlying Gaussian field. At the larger perturbation strengths considered, the Laplace perturbations yield larger mean maximum intensities and higher exceedance probabilities for the normalized intensity at the final simulation time, but smaller amplification relative to the initial maximum intensity.

papers.title: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-Improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: Discovering equations from data provides governing laws, constitutive relations and closure models for scientific understanding and prediction. Yet a method that succeeds on one system may fail on another or on noisy data, so discovery depends on expert trial and error. Unsuccessful searches can still reveal useful parts of an equation, but these clues must be recognized and combined. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for agent-guided equation discovery built on composable discovery and cumulative experience. Seven complementary equation discovery methods and shared computational modules form reusable building blocks, connected through a common equation representation. Researchers can launch discovery with one command and guide it with partially known equations. LegoSR Agent selects methods, revises searches using feedback and combines partial findings into new hypotheses. Its Experience Library consolidates graded outcomes into lessons that guide later tasks across equation families. Evaluation covers 134 algebraic regression problems, 40 ordinary differential equation targets and 25 partial differential equation problems at several noise levels, together with three case studies. papers.title: Attenuation of shoaling extreme wave crests by artificial salt marshes
papers.abstract: Laboratory experiments in a wave flume investigated the attenuation of shoaling extreme waves by artificial salt marshes placed immediately before an abrupt depth transition. Increasing vegetation density systematically reduced the excess kurtosis of the surface elevation distribution in the intermediate water depth regime. Nonetheless, attenuation exhibits a short saturation regime at low vegetation densities, whereas at very high densities, excess kurtosis decreases significantly across the gauges. However, kurtosis attenuation becomes ineffective as waves approach shallow-water conditions or as second-order nonlinear effects become significant. Furthermore, the highest experimental densities where the kurtosis is tamed exceed typical natural salt marsh stem densities. Thus, in natural settings, salt marshes are likely to provide only partial mitigation of extreme wave statistics in intermediate and shallow water depths, as the wave field retains some hazardous nonlinearity.

papers.abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of identifying the bottom-boundary of an ocean basin, particularly in the coastal region where shallow-water theory applies. Our main contribution is the development of an easy-to-implement observer-based approach of identifying the bottom-boundary profile from measurements of the free-surface. Furthermore, we prove that the true profile can be obtained by minimising the long-time observation-error as computed from the observer equations associated with a class of linear dispersive shallow water-wave models. Numerical simulations indicate the same optimisation problem can recover the true profile for the nonlinear versions of the same dispersive water-wave models.

papers.title: A Synergistic Assessment of Global Wind and Wave Energy Resources Using Satellite Altimetry
papers.venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
papers.abstract: The combined exploitation of marine wind and wave energy contributes to addressing pressing energy challenges. Satellite altimetry enables global synergistic assessment of these resources. Here, we utilize the longest altimeter observations available (Jason series, 1993–2024) to assess the spatiotemporal distribution, correlation, variability, and synergy of global wind and wave energy. Altimeter-derived wind speed and significant wave height were validated against buoy data, showing high consistency. Results indicate that wind and wave energy share similar spatiotemporal distributions. The Southern Ocean exhibits the most powerful and persistent resources, with moderate variability and correlation. Other energetic regions, including the Arabian Sea, North Atlantic, and North Pacific, show higher correlation and variability. papers.abstract: This work presents a methodology for identifying and reproducing critical wave events that induce extreme mooring line tension in floating offshore wind turbines. The approach begins with fully non-linear sea-state realisations, generated using a JONSWAP spectrum and propagated via a fully non-linear potential flow solver. papers.title: Hypothesize, Evaluate, Refine: A Scientific Agent for PDE Discovery with Unknown Spatial Coefficient Fields
papers.abstract: Discovering PDEs in heterogeneous media requires jointly identifying the governing operator and the unknown spatial fields that parameterize it. These tasks are coupled: changing field placement changes the differential law, while a sufficiently flexible field can conceal structural error on a single trajectory. We present Hypothesize, Evaluate, Refine for PDE Discovery (HER-PDE), a scientific-agent framework that discovers compositional PDE structure together with nonparametric, time-invariant coefficient fields. The Agent analyzes two noisy trajectories generated by different excitations, proposes complete expression-tree hypotheses, and combines creative structural exploration with local candidate refinement. Its Hypothesis Evaluation Interface (HEI) estimates only the fields explicitly declared in each hypothesis, never adds missing terms, and scores structures by bidirectional cross-excitation transfer. The selected law is subsequently audited on a sealed temporal interval. Across five controlled two-dimensional systems observed with 5 percent relative Gaussian state noise, the Agent recovers the generating operator in all five cases, including equivalent signed-field and product-rule parameterizations. Across nine unknown coefficient fields, the recovered fields attain a median Pearson correlation of approximately 0.85 and a median relative L2 error of approximately 0.28.

Beach scale tidal variations observed from satellite-derived shoreline time series
papers.abstract: Coastal tidal dynamics play a crucial role in a variety of biogeophysical processes, ranging from compound flooding to sediment transport. Satellite altimetry has revolutionized our understanding of ocean tides, but coastal regions remain challenging for satellite altimetry-based observations. In recent years, important efforts have been made to produce shoreline measurements from satellite optical imagery. These datasets raise the question of whether shoreline observations can resolve tidal dynamics at fine coastal scales. Here, we show that shoreline measurements provide fine-scale insights into tidal characteristics, demonstrating variability at beach scales across the Pacific Rim. We explore how both harmonic analysis and response-based methods can be applied to these data to study a range of tidal constituents. Our results are contrasted with in situ measurements and state-of-the-art models as well as with wide-swath satellite observations. We demonstrate that satellite-derived shoreline measurements are a valuable resource for tidal research, particularly for model validation and the study of tidal constituent variability in the coastal zone. Satellite-derived shoreline measurements can provide insights into coastal tidal dynamics and for the validation of models in the coastal zone, according to analyses using shoreline position data from around the Pacific Rim.

papers.abstract: The finite span and twist of wind turbine blades induce spanwise flow, along with a tip vortex. Conventional blade element theory, rooted in a two-dimensional assumption, cannot capture these spanwise effects. However, most existing three-dimensional (3-D) corrections neglect intrinsic geometric effects leading to inaccuracies near the tip and in non-rotating cases. To address this, we propose the 3-D geometric effects model incorporating axial and radial velocity factors (3-DGAR model), a physically consistent correction to blade element momentum theory. The model captures two fundamental phenomena: downwash that modifies the local effective angle of attack and tip pressure loss driven by radial velocity transport. A coherent physical pathway from the tip vortex to load reduction is established: the spanwise flow transports energy from the tip element into the tip vortex, reducing suction-side velocity and thereby weakening suction at the equivalent angle of attack. Furthermore, symbolic regression is then used to determine two unknown velocity factors from limited experimental data, serving as closure terms.
